body: The guard on approval requests looked complete: it counted them, refused bundled ones, and enforced the limit. Then a request reached the owner in a form the guard simply did not recognise, asking something that had already been decided months earlier. The lesson was not that the guard was weak — it was that it had been checking how many of one known shape could be asked, never whether other shapes existed, and its visible success is what kept anyone from asking.

Keeping private files out of a public project seemed to mean listing them as exclusions — with the nagging worry that the list itself advertises their names. Then a tool, doing exactly what its approved design said, published the assistant's private working folder. Adding those files to the exclusion list would not have helped: the real exposure was everything nobody had classified, which no list of known items can cover. So the direction flipped — exclude everything, justify each exception — and now forgetting makes something fail visibly instead of publishing quietly.
